title: Randi Weingarten and the American Federation of Teachers MUST REVERSE Their Decision on ChatGPTZero
author: Stefan Bauschard
summary: Bauschard, an AI-in-education writer, argues that the American Federation of Teachers' partnership with GPTZero to bring AI-writing detection into schools is a serious mistake. His case has several strands: detectors are demonstrably unreliable and easy to defeat, their false positives fall hardest on non-native English writers and special education students, and the policy invites lawsuits. He also attacks the survey the AFT commissioned to justify the program, saying its claim that students rarely use AI is implausible and does not show parents want detectors. His larger point is that public schools should be spending money on teacher AI training and redesigning assignments rather than policing plagiarism. The tone is openly angry and the piece is polemical, but it is a clear school-policy argument about a specific ed-tech product.
points: The central claim is that AI-writing detectors are inaccurate, easily defeated by small edits, and therefore unfit to ground discipline.
False positives are said to burden non-native English writers, weaker writers and special education students, who already face disproportionate discipline.
He questions the AFT's commissioned survey, noting that teachers' reports of no student AI use cannot be trusted when detection does not work.
He argues the money would be better spent training teachers to teach with AI and reinventing assignments for an AI world.
He charges that banning students from tools while teachers use them for lesson plans is untenable and that public schools risk falling behind private ones.
quotes: Because these detectors make percentage chance predictions based on the pattern in the analyzed text to determine if it was likely written by AI. Simple output patterns are more likely to be detected as “AI written” because AI output tends to follow simple patterns (this is explained in more detail here).
Who writes in simpler patterns? Non-native writers and students who are poor writers. This obviously also falls most heavily on particular classes and races.
This is so sad because what teachers need to be doing is learning how to teach with this technology in the classroom. They need to learn how to reinvent assignments for an AI world.
How would they know? Plagiarism detectors don’t work, and just because students don’t use them at school doesn’t mean they don’t use them at home.
Yes, penalizing students has consequences, and when it has a nonsense foundation, they sue you. This program is basically a lawsuit generator.
The kids are done with a world where they are banned from using technology that is essential to their future while their teachers use it to do their own work.
No one invested hundreds of billions of dollars in tools to write school essays, and this is honestly the least of the challenges we face as a society.
